This library provides PHP 8.6's [`Time\Duration`](https://wiki.php.net/rfc/duration_class) on PHP 8.2 to 8.5.
It also provides helpers for durations and [PSR-20](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-20/) clocks.

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{formatDuration, parseDuration, sec, toMs, toSecFloat};

$timeout = sec(1.5);

toMs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity); // 1500
toSecFloat($timeout); // 1.5
formatDuration($timeout); // 1.5s

$timeout = parseDuration($_ENV['HTTP_TIMEOUT'] ?? '1.5s');
```

## Installation

```shell
composer require thesis/time
```

This package requires PHP 8.2.2+ and runs on 32-bit and 64-bit PHP without extensions.
Below PHP 8.4 `\RoundingMode` comes from `symfony/polyfill-php84`.

## Time\Duration polyfill

`Time\Duration` is elapsed time with nanosecond precision: a timeout, a delay, a TTL. On PHP 8.2 to 8.5
the package declares `Time\Duration` and `Time\TimeException`, on PHP 8.6 the built-in classes work, so code written
for 8.6 runs on 8.2 as is. Here are the essentials, [the RFC](https://wiki.php.net/rfc/duration_class) describes
the whole class.

```php
use Time\Duration;

$ttl = Duration::fromMinutes(5);
$timeout = Duration::fromSeconds(1, nanoseconds: 500_000_000);
$delay = Duration::fromIso8601DurationString('PT1M30S');

$ttl->add($timeout);
$ttl->sub($timeout);
$timeout->multiplyBy(3);
$timeout->divideBy(2);
$timeout->negate();
$timeout->absolute();

Duration::compare($ttl, $timeout); // 1
$timeout < $ttl; // true

$timeout->seconds; // 1
$timeout->nanoseconds; // 500000000
$timeout->negative; // false
```

The factories are `fromNanoseconds()`, `fromMicroseconds()`, `fromMilliseconds()`, `fromSeconds()`, `fromMinutes()`
and `fromHours()`. The class is minimal on purpose: the factories take only non-negative ints, and nothing converts
a duration back to a number. The [functions](#functions) fill these gaps.

A duration spans about ±292 years, ±68 years on 32-bit PHP. A value out of range throws `Time\TimeException`.

The polyfill behaves as the class of PHP 8.6 down to the exception messages, compared with the original
on random input. What differs: `var_dump()` and an `(array)` cast show two more private properties,
reflection sees `__serialize()`, and a wrong call fails as with a userland method (extra arguments are ignored,
`null` for an int is a `TypeError` in coercive mode too).

## Functions

### Creating

Unlike the factories of the class, the functions take a negative value, and all but `ns()` a float,
rounded to the nearest nanosecond, half away from zero.

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{duration, hours, minutes, ms, ns, sec, us};

ns(15);
us(1.5);
ms(-250);
sec(90);
minutes(1.5);
hours(0.25);

duration(minutes: 1, sec: 30); // the sum of the parts
```

A value out of range throws `Time\TimeException`, `NAN` and `INF` throw `\ValueError`.

### Converting to int

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{sec, toHours, toMinutes, toMs, toNs, toSec, toUs};

$duration = sec(90.5);

toNs($duration);                                    // 90500000000
toUs($duration, RoundingMode::TowardsZero);         // 90500000
toMs($duration, RoundingMode::TowardsZero);         // 90500
toSec($duration, RoundingMode::TowardsZero);        // 90
toSec($duration, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity);   // 91
toMinutes($duration, RoundingMode::TowardsZero);    // 1
toHours($duration, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity); // 1
```

`toNs()` is exact. The others take a `\RoundingMode` and have no default: the right one depends on what the number
means. Round a timeout, a TTL or an interval up with `PositiveInfinity`, so that it never expires early and a positive
one never becomes the `0` that many APIs take as "no limit", see [the table](#passing-to-other-apis) below.
A deadline that has passed still gives `0` or less: take `max(1, ...)` or check it with `$remaining > sec(0)` first.
Drop the fraction of elapsed time with `TowardsZero`.

On 64-bit PHP every duration fits in an int of any unit, nanoseconds too. On 32-bit PHP an int holds 2.1 seconds
of nanoseconds, 35 minutes of microseconds, 24 days of milliseconds, and a larger result throws `Time\TimeException`.
The float conversions never throw.

### Converting to float

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{sec, toHoursFloat, toMinutesFloat, toMsFloat, toNsFloat, toSecFloat, toUsFloat};

$duration = sec(90.5);

toNsFloat($duration);      // 90500000000.0
toUsFloat($duration);      // 90500000.0
toMsFloat($duration);      // 90500.0
toSecFloat($duration);     // 90.5
toMinutesFloat($duration); // 1.5083333333333333
toHoursFloat($duration);   // 0.025138888888888888
```

For APIs that take float seconds, like the timeout of `stream_socket_client()`, and for metrics and logs.
The result is the float nearest to the duration up to 104 days (2^53 nanoseconds), and at most a unit
in the last place off above. `toNsFloat()` is for 32-bit PHP, where `toNs()` throws.

### Passing to other APIs

What to pass where a timeout or a TTL is a number, and what `0` means there: rarely "at once".

| Where                              | Pass                                              | `0` means                   |
|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| curl, `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS`         | `toMs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)`  | **no limit**                |
| curl, `CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT_MS`  | `toMs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)`  | the default, 300 seconds    |
| Guzzle, `timeout`                  | `toSecFloat($timeout)`                            | **no limit**                |
| Guzzle, `connect_timeout`          | `toSecFloat($timeout)`                            | 300 seconds                 |
| Symfony HttpClient, `max_duration` | `toSecFloat($timeout)`                            | **no limit**                |
| Symfony HttpClient, `timeout`      | `toSecFloat($timeout)`                            | times out at once           |
| PDO, `PDO::ATTR_TIMEOUT`           | `toSec($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)` | **no limit**, not in SQLite |
| `stream_set_timeout()`             | `toUs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)`  | a read does not wait        |
| PSR-16, `$ttl`                     | `toSec($ttl, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)`     | the item is deleted         |
| Postgres, `statement_timeout`      | `toMs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity)`  | **no limit**                |

- **curl.** `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` and `CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT` take whole seconds: `toSec()` with the same mode.
- **Guzzle, Symfony HttpClient.** Float seconds need no mode, but with curl both turn them into whole milliseconds
  and drop the fraction: 0.9 ms becomes `0`, no limit. Where a timeout can be that short (the time left
  until a deadline), pass `max(0.001, toSecFloat($timeout))`. `timeout` of Symfony limits the wait between
  two chunks, the whole request is limited by `max_duration`.
- **PDO.** The time to connect in MySQL and Postgres, where `0` waits as long as the system does. In SQLite
  the wait for a locked database, where `0` fails at once.
- **`stream_set_timeout()`.** The microseconds, with `0` seconds before them: PHP carries whole seconds over,
  `stream_set_timeout($stream, 0, toUs($timeout, RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity))`. No limit is `-1` second.
- **PSR-16.** A negative TTL deletes the item too, `null` is the default TTL of the cache.
- **Postgres.** A number without a unit is milliseconds, also in `lock_timeout`
  and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.

### Checking, comparing, multiplying, dividing

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{isZero, multiply, ratio, sec};

isZero($duration);
$duration->negative;
$duration > sec(0);
$elapsed >= $timeout;

min($a, $b, $c);
max($a, $b, $c);

multiply($delay, 2); // exact
multiply($delay, 1.5); // rounded to the nearest nanosecond
multiply($delay, -1);

ratio($elapsed, $total); // 0.25, a progress
ratio($cpuTime, $elapsed); // 0.8, a load
(int) ratio($elapsed, $interval); // the intervals that have passed
```

`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `<=>` compare durations by value, on PHP 8.6 and with the polyfill,
and so do `min()`, `max()` and `sort()` of PHP. Check zero with `isZero()`, not with `==`: PHP CS Fixer
and others make it `===`, which compares the objects.

`ratio()` divides a duration by a duration, which the class does not. The result is the float nearest
to the quotient while both are up to 104 days, so durations that divide evenly give a whole number.
A zero divisor throws `\DivisionByZeroError`.

### Rounding

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{formatDuration, minutes, ms, roundDurationTo};

formatDuration($elapsed); // 1.234567891s
formatDuration(roundDurationTo($elapsed, ms(1), RoundingMode::HalfAwayFromZero)); // 1.235s

roundDurationTo($timeout, minutes(1), RoundingMode::PositiveInfinity);
```

`roundDurationTo()` rounds a duration to a multiple of a unit, like `Duration.Round()` and `Duration.Truncate()` of Go.
The unit is any positive duration, `ms(1500)` too, anything else throws `\ValueError`. The `\RoundingMode`
has no default, as in the [conversions to int](#converting-to-int).

### Formatting and parsing

`formatDuration()` writes a duration like `Duration.String()` of Go, and `parseDuration()` reads it back
in the grammar of `time.ParseDuration()`: for logs, and for a timeout in an environment variable, a config
or an option of a command.

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{duration, formatDuration, parseDuration};

formatDuration(duration(hours: 1, minutes: 2, sec: 3.5)); // 1h2m3.5s
formatDuration(parseDuration('90s')); // 1m30s

parseDuration('1h2m3.5s');
parseDuration('250ms');
parseDuration('-1.5h');
parseDuration('0');
```

A string is numbers with a unit each (`h`, `m`, `s`, `ms`, `us` or `µs`, `ns`) after an optional sign, with a fraction
in any of them and no spaces. Only `0` has no unit. A number is a float converted like the function of its unit:
`parseDuration('1.5h')` is `hours(1.5)`. So a fraction of a nanosecond is rounded, while Go drops it,
and a number is as precise as a float, to 15 significant digits. A string that is not a duration
or is out of range throws `Time\TimeException`.

### Points in time

`durationBetween()` and `shiftTime()` count elapsed time between timestamps, so a change of the UTC offset (DST)
does not count. `shiftTime()` drops the nanoseconds below a microsecond, which `DateTimeImmutable` cannot hold.

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{durationBetween, shiftTime};

$expiresAt = shiftTime($clock->now(), $ttl);
$retainedSince = shiftTime($clock->now(), $retention->negate());
$elapsed = durationBetween($startedAt, $clock->now());
```

`roundTimeTo()` rounds a time to a multiple of a unit since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC: rounded down, the times
of one window give its start, a key for a limit or a metric.

```php
use function Thesis\Time\{minutes, roundTimeTo};

$now = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-01 12:34:56 Europe/Moscow');

roundTimeTo($now, minutes(5), RoundingMode::NegativeInfinity); // 2026-01-01 12:30:00 Europe/Moscow
```

The functions use multiples of elapsed time. With `hours(24)`, the multiples fall at UTC midnight,
whatever the time zone of the time, which is kept. The unit is positive and of whole microseconds,
anything else throws `\ValueError`.

`Time.Round()` and `Time.Truncate()` of Go do the same from the year 1: the results match for a unit
that divides a day, but a week starts on Thursday here and on Monday there.

The ends of int64 timestamps (the year ±292 billion) are out of reach: `shiftTime()` beyond them gives a wrong time
or an error, as `DateTimeImmutable::add()` wraps around there, and `roundTimeTo()` within 512 seconds of them
may give a time that is not a multiple of the unit.

## PSR-20 clocks

`WallClock` and `FrozenClock` implement
[`Psr\Clock\ClockInterface`](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-20/#21-clockinterface).

```php
use Thesis\Time\{FrozenClock, WallClock};
use function Thesis\Time\sec;

$clock = new WallClock(); // the system time in the default time zone
$clock = new WallClock(new DateTimeZone('UTC'));

$clock = new FrozenClock(new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC')); // for tests
$clock->advance(sec(30));
$clock->now = new DateTimeImmutable('2027-01-01 00:00:00 UTC');
```

`FrozenClock` moves only when told: by `advance()` or by assigning `$clock->now`.

## Stopwatch

`Thesis\Time\Stopwatch` measures real elapsed time on the system's monotonic clock, even under virtual time.
Each reading is a `Time\Duration`.

```php
$watch = Thesis\Time\Stopwatch::start();
$records = readRecords();
$readTime = $watch->lap();
writeRecords($records);
$writeTime = $watch->lap();
$total = $watch->elapsed();
```
